title: Demoralized Men
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Renn analyzes an Institute for Family Studies survey of 2,000 American men aged 18-29, revealing how Gen Z males perceive adulthood, career, education, and relationships. The research shows a significant shift in what young men consider markers of adulthood: while full-time employment remains common, financial independence has emerged as a more valued milestone. The survey reveals striking gaps in college attainment between liberal and conservative Gen Z men (liberals twice as likely to hold degrees) and demonstrates that family structure significantly impacts educational outcomes. Notably, the research indicates that the majority of young men fear approaching women for dating, a reversal from earlier manosphere approaches focused on overcoming approach anxiety. The piece concludes that young men hunger for positive definitions of masculinity centered on strength and leadership, not merely sacrifice and service.
points: Gen Z men prioritize financial independence over traditional full-time employment, reflecting broader cultural shift toward entrepreneurship and autonomy.
Educational attainment among Gen Z men shows stark partisan divide: liberals are twice as likely to hold college degrees as conservatives.
Family structure remains a powerful predictor of educational success: children from intact families are three times more likely to hold degrees.
Majority of young men fear asking women on dates, representing cultural shift away from earlier manosphere approaches to overcoming approach anxiety.
Young men seek positive definitions of masculinity emphasizing strength and leadership, not merely sacrifice and service.
quotes: We see here that the majority of young men are afraid to ask women out. Most men have long been hesitant to ask women on dates. One of the biggest planks in the manosphere was about men forcing themselves to approach women in order to overcome “approach anxiety.” Their mantra was “always be approaching.” Helping men overcome nervousness here - and frame rejection as nothing shameful but something that happens to basically all men the majority of the time if they are actually asking people out - was one of the successful self-improvement items on their list.

The study emphasizes men agreeing with the idea that manhood is about sacrifice. I find it more interesting that an even higher percentage of men said it included “strength” and “leadership.” Almost everyone agrees that manhood involves sacrifice and service. But our society too often reduced it to that. I think this survey shows men are hungry for a definition in manhood that has more positive elements in it, like strength and leadership.
